title: The Valley Beneath the Velvet Cloak

passage.title: The Valley Beneath the Velvet Cloak
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Bank
passage.text:
After the museum halls closed at dusk, Clara wheeled the walnut easel into the quiet studio. On the padded ledge rested an old oil portrait of a stern duke dressed in a heavy black cloak. Over four hundred winters, candle smoke and yellow varnish had dimmed the canvas into a murky shadow. Yet Clara's mentor, Dr. Vance, suspected that the stiff nobleman was not the first scene painted on this linen. Before mixing a single drop of mild solvent, Clara needed to peer through the dark surface without scraping a thread.

She switched off the ceiling lamps and aimed a violet wand across the duke's broad shoulder. Under the purple beam, old tree-resin varnish glowed with a milky green haze except along one strange ridge. Near the bottom corner, a jagged patch of dark blue paint refused to glow at all, proving it came from a later brush. Under the beam of the violet lamp, the cracked varnish on the duke's cloak was filmed by Clara before a cotton swab touched the canvas. That map of light and shadow told her right where later hands had patched the picture.

Next, Clara wheeled the heat camera into place on its tall iron track. Unlike violet light, which bounces off the top varnish, gentle infrared waves slip right through thin layers of oil paint. As the scanner crept across the duke's chest, gray lines began to bloom on Clara's monitor screen. Neither Clara nor Dr. Vance spoke as the stern nobleman vanished on the glass display.

In place of the dark velvet coat, a sunlit Tuscan valley stretched between two rows of cypress trees. A stone bridge arched over a winding river where a shepherd leaned on his staff beside three grazing sheep. Quick charcoal strokes along the hills showed where the young artist had sketched the valley from life. Back then, fine linen cost so much gold that poor painters often scraped down unsold scenes to paint rich patrons.

Clara rolled a tiny cotton swab in mild cedar oil and touched the edge of the duke's sleeve. She could not erase the historic portrait, which belonged to the city museum, nor would she conceal the lost valley again. Instead, she and Dr. Vance planned a side-by-side display for the spring gallery show. Visitors would view the clean portrait beside a full-sized print of the hidden river. For the first time in four centuries, both the proud patron and the humble valley would share the light.

tier2Words.definition: Serious, strict, and unsmiling in expression
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old English 'styrne' meaning strict or severe
tier2Words.contextClue: The duke in the heavy black cloak looked serious and unyielding.

tier2Words.definition: A liquid able to dissolve other substances, such as old dirt or varnish
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'solvere' meaning to loosen or dissolve
tier2Words.contextClue: Art workers use a mild cleaning liquid to dissolve old yellow varnish.

tier2Words.definition: Wealthy supporters who pay artists to create paintings or sculptures
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'patronus' meaning protector or sponsor
tier2Words.contextClue: Poor painters reused fine linen when wealthy buyers paid them to paint portraits.

tier2Words.definition: To hide something or keep it from being seen
tier2Words.contextClue: Clara refused to hide the lost valley again, choosing instead to display its print.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Under the beam of the violet lamp, the cracked varnish on the duke's cloak was filmed by Clara before a cotton swab touched the canvas."

Who performed the action of filming the cracked varnish in this sentence?

options.text: The duke wearing the heavy black cloak
options.childFeedback: Careful—the duke's cloak is part of the painting being examined in Paragraph 2, not the person operating the camera.

options.text: Dr. Vance, who mixed the mild solvent
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Dr. Vance joins Clara later in Paragraph 3, whereas Paragraph 2 says the cracked varnish was filmed by Clara.

options.text: The violet lamp shining above the easel
options.childFeedback: Watch out—the violet lamp provided the light in Paragraph 2, but the words 'by Clara' name who actually filmed the varnish.

options.text: Clara, working in the quiet studio
options.childFeedback: Spot on! In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'by Clara' right after 'was filmed' shows that Clara performed the action of filming the cracked varnish.

questions.provingSentenceText: Under the beam of the violet lamp, the cracked varnish on the duke's cloak was filmed by Clara before a cotton swab touched the canvas.
questions.childTip: Spot on! In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'by Clara' right after 'was filmed' shows that Clara performed the action of filming the cracked varnish.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, 'the cracked varnish on the duke's cloak' receives the action ('was filmed'). The agent following 'by' is 'Clara.'
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 2, find the action phrase 'was filmed' and look right after 'by' to see who did the filming.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 5:

"She could not erase the historic portrait, which belonged to the city museum, nor would she conceal the lost valley again."

What does the word "conceal" most nearly mean as used in this sentence?

options.text: Sell to a wealthy duke
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 5 states that the portrait already belonged to the city museum, and Clara was restoring it, not selling it.

options.text: Paint over with bright green varnish
options.childFeedback: Watch out—this choice mixes up the milky green glow of old varnish in Paragraph 2 with what Clara decides to do in Paragraph 5.

options.text: Keep hidden from view
options.childFeedback: Spot on! In Paragraph 5, Clara refuses to 'conceal' the lost valley again and instead hangs a full-size print of it beside the portrait so everyone can see it.

options.text: Display in the center of the hall
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice gives the exact opposite meaning! Clara displays the print so that she will NOT conceal (hide) the valley anymore.

questions.provingSentenceText: She could not erase the historic portrait, which belonged to the city museum, nor would she conceal the lost valley again.
questions.childTip: Spot on! In Paragraph 5, Clara refuses to 'conceal' the lost valley again and instead hangs a full-size print of it beside the portrait so everyone can see it.
questions.parentExplanation: Because the valley had been buried beneath the duke's portrait for four hundred years, Clara refuses to 'conceal' (hide) it again and instead exhibits a print beside the painting.
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 5, notice what Clara does next: she puts a print of the valley on display so it will not be hidden anymore.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 2, how does Clara know that a patch near the bottom corner of the painting was added by a later brush?

options.text: The dark blue patch refuses to glow with the milky green haze of old varnish.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraph 2 explains that old tree-resin varnish glows milky green under the purple lamp, so the dark blue patch that refused to glow had to be a newer repair.

options.text: The later artist signed his name in charcoal strokes across the stone bridge.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—the stone bridge is part of the hidden charcoal sketch underneath in Paragraph 4, and no signature is mentioned.

options.text: A cotton swab dipped in cedar oil immediately dissolved the black cloak.
options.childFeedback: Careful—Paragraph 2 states that Clara filmed the varnish under the violet lamp BEFORE a cotton swab ever touched the canvas.

options.text: The walnut easel tilted forward when the heat camera touched the corner.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—the walnut easel never tilts in the story, and the heat camera in Paragraph 3 does not touch the canvas.

questions.provingSentenceText: Near the bottom corner, a jagged patch of dark blue paint refused to glow at all, proving it came from a later brush.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraph 2 explains that old tree-resin varnish glows milky green under the purple lamp, so the dark blue patch that refused to glow had to be a newer repair.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 explains that genuine old tree-resin varnish glows with a milky green haze under the beam; because the dark blue patch refused to glow at all, Clara knew it was a newer repair.
questions.retryHint: Look in Paragraph 2 for the sentence that explains what the dark blue patch did under the purple beam.

questions.prompt: Why does the author include the historical detail about the high cost of fine linen in Paragraph 4?

options.text: To criticize Clara for using mild cedar oil on the duke's velvet sleeve
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Dr. Vance never criticizes Clara; in Paragraph 4 they work together with excitement as the hidden sketch appears.

options.text: To show that the city museum could not afford to buy new frames for the spring show
options.childFeedback: Careful—Paragraph 4 explains that the young artist four hundred years ago was too poor to buy fresh linen, not that the modern museum lacked frames.

options.text: To prove that cypress trees only grew near wealthy towns in Italy
options.childFeedback: Watch out—cypress trees are simply part of the hidden valley drawing in Paragraph 4, not proof of where trees grew in Italy.

options.text: To explain why the young artist painted the duke's portrait over an earlier valley scene
options.childFeedback: Spot on! The last sentence of Paragraph 4 explains that when a wealthy duke paid for a portrait, a poor young artist had to paint right over his own earlier valley canvas.

questions.provingSentenceText: Back then, fine linen cost so much gold that poor painters often scraped down unsold scenes to paint rich patrons.
questions.childTip: Spot on! The last sentence of Paragraph 4 explains that when a wealthy duke paid for a portrait, a poor young artist had to paint right over his own earlier valley canvas.
questions.parentExplanation: The detail about the cost of fine linen explains the mystery at the heart of the story: why a sunlit Tuscan valley was painted over with a wealthy duke's portrait.
questions.retryHint: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 4 to see why poor artists reused linen they had already painted.

questions.prompt: Part A: Why do Clara and Dr. Vance use two different kinds of light—violet light and infrared waves—before cleaning the painting?

options.text: The ceiling lamps in the studio are broken after the museum halls close at dusk.
options.childFeedback: Not quite—Paragraph 1 mentions that Clara turned off the ceiling lamps on purpose so she could see how the violet beam reacted with the varnish.

options.text: Violet light melts away candle smoke, while infrared waves dry the wet cedar oil on the sleeve.
options.childFeedback: Careful—neither light melts smoke or dries oil; Paragraph 2 says Clara used a cotton swab with mild cedar oil to clean the grime.

options.text: Violet light reveals surface repairs in the top varnish, while infrared waves pass through oil paint to show the sketch underneath.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain that violet light bounces off the top varnish to show surface repairs, while infrared waves pass through oil paint to reveal the charcoal sketch underneath.

options.text: Both lights are needed to burn off the dark velvet cloak so only the river remains.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 5 states that Clara could not erase the historic portrait, and the gentle light beams never burn the canvas.

questions.provingSentenceText: Unlike violet light, which bounces off the top varnish, gentle infrared waves slip right through thin layers of oil paint.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain that violet light bounces off the top varnish to show surface repairs, while infrared waves pass through oil paint to reveal the charcoal sketch underneath.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain that violet light reflects off the top varnish to expose surface patches, whereas infrared waves penetrate thin layers of oil paint to reveal the hidden sketch.
questions.retryHint: Look at Paragraph 3 for the sentence that contrasts what violet light does with what infrared waves do.

options.text: "Over four hundred winters, candle smoke and yellow varnish had dimmed the canvas into a murky shadow."

options.text: "Unlike violet light, which bounces off the top varnish, gentle infrared waves slip right through thin layers of oil paint."
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This quote from Paragraph 3 directly proves Question 5 by contrasting how violet light bounces off top varnish while infrared waves slip through oil paint.

options.text: "A stone bridge arched over a winding river where a shepherd leaned on his staff beside three grazing sheep."
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this detail from Paragraph 4 describes what the hidden valley sketch looked like rather than how the two lights worked.

options.text: "Clara rolled a tiny cotton swab in mild cedar oil and touched the edge of the duke's sleeve."
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this line from Paragraph 2 describes Clara testing a cotton swab with cedar oil, not how the violet and infrared lights worked.
